podcast.title: Phonograph Invention (1876)
podcast.body: Around 1876, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph, a device for recording and reproducing sound using cylindrical tubes. This invention marked a foundational moment in audio history, though his initial cylindrical format would later be deemed a significant failure in the evolution of music formats. "Thomas Edison inventaba el phonógrafo."

podcast.title: First Playable Recording (1877)
podcast.body: Thomas Edison made the first playable recording in 1877, following his invention of the telephone. He aimed to explore if telephone audio could be preserved for later reproduction. His device consisted of a rotating cylinder, a recording needle, and a diaphragm that translated sound pressure into analog indentations on the cylinder. "Este proceso fue primero colocado en 1877 por Thomas Edison."

podcast.title: Talking Machine - First Demonstration (1877)
podcast.body: Thomas Edison's talking machine was one of the first devices capable of capturing sound, demonstrating this capability in 1877. It had a recording limit of approximately three minutes, which subsequently influenced the standard length of popular songs. "Thomas Edison's talking machine, first demonstrated in 1877... were the first machines able to capture sound up to three minutes at a time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cylindrical Format - First Major Failure
podcast.body: Thomas Edison initially developed his phonograph using cylindrical tubes, a decision driven by a complex technical challenge with flat discs. While cylinders allowed for a constant angular speed with linear needle movement, they proved impractical for storing sound, leading to their abandonment and marking them as the first major failure in music formats. "Esos cilindros, evidentemente no lo usamos por lo que el primer grandísimo fracaso que tuvo el formato de la música."

podcast.title: Flat Disc Speed Problem (Late 19th Century)
podcast.body: Thomas Edison's initial attempt to use flat discs for recording faced a critical technical hurdle: he observed that while a vinyl disc spins at a constant angular speed, the needle's reproduction speed is not constant. This complex issue led him to temporarily set aside the flat disc concept in favor of cylindrical recordings. "Thomas Edison se dio cuenta de que el problema del disco plano era que la velocidad angular no era la misma que la velocidad de reproducción de la aguja."

podcast.title: Phonograph Invention and Analog Voice Recording
podcast.body: Edison designed a system where he spoke into a diaphragm, which moved a recording needle. As a cylinder was turned, the pressure from his voice was imprinted as analog indentations onto the cylinder's surface, creating a physical record of his speech. This invention marked the beginning of sound recording technology. "Edison habló de la presión de la presión, mientras se llevó el recorregimiento a un constante de la presión y, como lo han perdido, la presión de las sonrías se imprintó en una propuesta indentación que fue analógico para el recorregimiento de su voz."

xref.title: Early Wax Cylinder Recording (1896)
xref.body: The Peerless Orchestra's medley of hit songs was recorded in 1896 on a wax cylinder, serving as a demonstration of Thomas Edison's phonograph technology. This early recording exemplifies how music could "now be captured and enjoyed wherever and whenever anyone wished" thanks to Edison's invention. "From 1896, the peerless orchestra and a wax cylinder recording that was made using Thomas Edison's phonograph technology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unique Recording Process
xref.body: Due to the technical limitations of Thomas Edison's wax cylinders, which were impossible to reproduce, every cylinder was a master recording. Johnson, with his strong voice, could be recorded by up to five machines simultaneously, and he would often repeat a song 50 times a day to produce enough copies. "So in other words, every single cylinder had to be recorded individually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
